h1: Why some beers make spicy food hotter
title: Why Some Beers Make Spicy Food Hotter | Craft Beer School
desc: Why bitter, strong and fizzy beers make chilli feel hotter, which beers calm the burn and how to pair beer with fiery Indian dishes.
teaser: That 8% double IPA did not cool your Andhra chicken. It turned up the heat. Here is why, plus what to order instead.
standfirst: Beer and spicy food seem made for each other, especially in India. Some pairings soothe the burn while others make it fiercer. The difference comes down to bitterness, alcohol, carbonation and sweetness.
sections:
The heat in chilli comes from capsaicin. It does not stimulate taste buds in the usual way. It triggers pain receptors in the mouth that normally respond to heat, which is why chilli feels hot rather than tasting of anything in particular.

Capsaicin dissolves in fat and in alcohol, but hardly at all in water. That is why a glass of water barely helps, while a spoonful of curd or a sip of lassi does. Keep that in mind and the rest of this guide makes sense.

Heat also builds. The first bite of a laal maas is rarely the hottest. By the tenth, your mouth is primed and everything feels sharper, including the beer. A pairing that seemed fine at the start of the meal can feel harsh by the end.

Hop bitterness and chilli heat amplify each other. A highly bitter beer makes the burn feel stronger. The burn in turn makes the bitterness feel harsher. The two pile up on the palate.

This is the most common pairing mistake. A big, bitter West Coast IPA at 60 IBU or more seems like a bold match for a fiery curry, but it often makes both taste aggressive. Our guide to bitterness perception explains why bitterness changes so much with what you eat alongside it.

Alcohol dissolves capsaicin, so in theory it should help. In practice, strong beers carry their own warmth. Higher alcohol tends to make the burn feel sharper while you drink. A 9% imperial stout with a vindaloo is a lot of heat in one mouthful.

Carbonation has an effect too. Carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid in the mouth, which gives that prickle on the tongue. Highly carbonated beers can make chilli feel livelier. Lower carbonation feels gentler. Our guide to carbonation levels by style shows where common beers sit.

Fizz is not all bad news, though. Bubbles scrub the palate between bites, which is why a crisp lager feels refreshing with fried snacks. The trouble starts when high carbonation, high bitterness and high strength arrive together in one glass.

The beers that work best with very spicy food share a few traits: modest bitterness, moderate strength and a touch of malt sweetness or body.

  • Wheat beers. A hefeweizen or witbier is soft, low in bitterness and lightly fruity. Coriander in a witbier echoes Indian spice.
  • Malty lagers. A Vienna lager, helles or Märzen gives bready sweetness without much bite.
  • Amber and brown ales. Caramel malt flavour stands up to bold spice and softens the edges.
  • Milk stout. Lactose sweetness and a creamy body can tame heat surprisingly well.

Serve them properly cold. A chilled beer feels soothing even when it is not dissolving any capsaicin.

Indian chilli heat varies enormously, so match the beer to the dish rather than to the cuisine.

Andhra chilli chicken or anything with Guntur chillies brings sharp, direct heat. A wheat beer or a helles keeps things manageable. Chettinad chicken is aromatic as well as hot, with black pepper and fennel. An amber ale or a Vienna lager matches the toasted spice.

Goan vindaloo has vinegar tang alongside its heat. A malty Märzen or a slightly sweet brown ale balances the acidity. Laal maas from Rajasthan is rich and fiery. A milk stout or a brown ale has the body to cope.

Our wider guide on Indian food and beer pairing covers milder dishes too. These are suggestions, not rules. Your own taste and your tolerance for heat decide what works.

The easiest way to understand all this is to try it. Order a bitter IPA and a wheat beer with the same spicy dish and switch between them. The difference is usually obvious within a few bites.

Describing that difference precisely is harder. Why did one beer feel harsher? Was it the bitterness, the alcohol or the fizz? Pulling those sensations apart is exactly the skill trained tasters work on. Once you can do it, pairing stops being guesswork.

Keep a glass of water on the table anyway. Eat plenty too. Spicy food makes people drink faster, so pace yourself.
faqs: Why does IPA make spicy food hotter?
Hop bitterness and chilli heat amplify each other. A bitter IPA makes the burn feel stronger, while the heat makes the bitterness feel harsher.
What beer goes best with very spicy food?
Beers with low bitterness, moderate strength and some malt sweetness. Wheat beers, malty lagers, amber ales and milk stouts are good choices.
Does water help with chilli heat?
Not much. Capsaicin barely dissolves in water. Dairy such as curd or lassi helps more.
